assessment_summary: A strong nationwide geo-randomized field experiment assigns Facebook video fundraising to 7,686 German postal codes and aggregates outcome data across all giving channels. The design credibly estimates ITT effects on total donations and frequency, includes randomization inference, sensitivity to post-period length, and checks for spillovers and heterogeneity. Key limitations: (1) Interference across postal codes is likely; while neighbor-treatment shares are modeled post hoc, spillovers make main ITT estimates lower bounds and complicate interpretation. (2) Outcomes are PLZ-day aggregates with winsorization at €1,000; aggregation may mask skew/variance dynamics, and robust SEs may not fully address spatial correlation. (3) Competition effects rely on online-only data with pretreatment imbalances, DiD adjustments, and overlapping sources; offline giving to competitors is unobserved, so crowd-out magnitudes are uncertain. (4) Deviations from preregistration (added blocking and a second treatment arm) are transparent but weaken ex ante commitments. (5) Profitability hinges on assumed lifetime value multipliers and excludes creative/overhead costs; CIs are wide. (6) Video-content and allocation comparisons are underpowered; several effects are marginal (p≈0.1) and multiple hypotheses lack adjustment. (7) Replication is constrained by restricted data access and semi-aggregated ad metrics in one arm. Despite these caveats, the identification and practical insights are valuable.

This is a timely, careful meta-analysis of RCTs on interventions to reduce meat and animal product (MAP) consumption, prioritizing consumption outcomes measured at least one day post-treatment and handling dependence via robust variance estimation. The authors transparently separate RPM-only from net-MAP outcomes, conduct multiple publication-bias adjustments (including worst-case checks), and provide open code, data, and containerized workflows. Main findings—small pooled effects that attenuate toward zero after bias correction—are communicated clearly and cautiously. Key limitations: the customized search and several inclusion/exclusion decisions were made post hoc, inviting selection subjectivity; data extraction and effect-size coding were done by a single coder without interrater checks; risk-of-bias assessment is limited (no structured RoB tool; little detail on allocation concealment, attrition, masking). Effect-size conversions mix Glass’s Δ and pooled SD; “unspecified nulls” are set to 0.01 (not 0), potentially biasing upward. Handling of clustering/cross-over correlations and repeated measures is not fully specified, and follow-up duration heterogeneity is not modeled as a moderator. Outcome measures remain heterogeneous and often self-reported, and SMDs are not translated into practical units (grams/emissions). Choice-architecture evidence is sparse, constraining inference. Minor editorial redundancies appear in the abstract.

This preregistered, PRISMA-consistent meta-analysis synthesizes a large RCT-only evidence base and applies appropriate multi-effect methods (RVE; MLRE) with useful subgrouping. Key issues: (i) Very high between-study heterogeneity (I2 ≈ 80–95%) with limited moderator explanatory power, making pooled g estimates hard to generalize; design moderators (e.g., “plus” components, targeting) are coarse and potentially confounded by region/implementer. (ii) Multiplicity and dependence: numerous outcomes per study raise risks of overweighting prolific studies; inclusion of both aggregate indices and their components may double-count constructs; weighting rules and any per-study caps are not fully specified. (iii) Missing or terse methodological details: assumed rho in RVE, handling of cluster RCTs in effect-size/variance computation, small-study/publication-bias diagnostics, and a transparent risk-of-bias assessment. (iv) Outcome harmonization: combining binary, index, and continuous measures into SMDs reduces interpretability; agency measures vary in validity. (v) Cost-benefit synthesis is sparse/heterogeneous and largely household-focused, rarely incorporating women-specific benefits; no formal meta-analytic synthesis of costs. (vi) External validity/time: LMIC focus is apt but language coverage yielded few non-English studies; follow-up horizons are short. (vii) Minor internal inconsistencies (e.g., public works g reported as 0.273 vs 0.127; unusual CI for decision-making) suggest minor reporting errors. Data/code availability is promised but not fully open (extraction form withheld).
